descripcion: English speakers soften opinions far more than Spanish speakers do. *That's wrong* is grammatically perfect and lands as rude; *I'm not sure that's right* says the same thing and keeps the conversation going. This is not politeness for its own sake: a softened claim is easier to defend, because you have not committed to more than you can support.

filas: A bit heavy, don't you think?
cuadroReferencia.notaPie: One or two per opinion. Three or more and it stops sounding careful and starts sounding evasive.

ejemplos.texto: *It's a bit rich for me, but that might just be my taste.*
*I'd say it needs a little more salt.*
*It's not really what I expected, to be honest.*

notas: *A bit* before a negative adjective is the single most useful softener in spoken English: *a bit dry*, *a bit late*, *a bit expensive*.
*To be honest* and *to be fair* soften rather than emphasise, which surprises learners.
Never soften a fact. *The restaurant might close at eleven* when you know it does sounds evasive rather than careful.

contraste.es: A plain Spanish opinion (eso es un error) translated literally (that's a mistake) often sounds harsher in English than intended. Adding a softener (I think that might be a mistake) brings it to the intended level.
contraste.de: German softens with particles (das ist wohl nicht ganz richtig), which disappear in translation and leave that's wrong. English needs a lexical softener: I'm not sure that's quite right.
contraste.it: A plain Italian statement (è sbagliato) becomes that's wrong, which sounds harsh in English. A softener (I'm not sure that's quite right) brings it to the intended level.
contraste.fr: C'est faux becomes that's false or that's wrong, which sounds harsh in English. A softener (I'm not sure that's quite right) brings it to the intended level.
contraste.pt: Isso está errado becomes that's wrong, which sounds harsh in English. A softener (I'm not sure that's quite right) brings it to the intended level.

errores: Saying nothing at all instead of disagreeing, which is the opposite over-correction.
Stacking: *I think maybe it could possibly be a bit…*
Softening a fact or a number.
*I'm not agree* — the fossilised error worth naming once.

redemittel.expresion: It might just be my taste.

autochequeo: Any opinion with three or more stacked?
Did I soften a fact by mistake?
Would a British listener find any sentence blunt?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on hedging and softening. (1) Mark each softener and say whether it fits. (2) Mark every flat opinion that an English speaker would have softened. (3) Flag any stacking. (4) Flag any fact I softened by mistake. Do not correct anything else.
